rv.q: There is an audience for this sentimental piece, I think, given the relative paucity of sincere musicals this season.
With the exception of its Cee Cee, alas, almost everything about Beaches is C-minus at best.

How long have I and no doubt many others waited to see that bizarre number – part of a downtown avant-garde musical starring Midler's character, ambitious singer Cee Cee Bloom – live on stage only to be so cruelly denied. That it is replaced by such bland muzak which makes the disappointment sting all the more.

This musical has been bobbing around the US and Canada since the Obama Administration, and has finally docked during Broadway's low tide. So not only is its music rather long in the tooth, but the score with some true clunkers also works very hard not to venture too far from the soft synth 1980s sounds of "Wind Beneath My Wings.
So it is absolutely bizarre that 'Beaches' the musical is a spectacularly unaffecting experience.
Sadly there's little wind beneath this uninspired musical's thin and tattered wings.
Beaches is that rare new musical based on well-known intellectual property that manages to exceed our hopes.

The witty dialogue known from the movie is there from the jump, with young versions of Cee Cee and Bertie (played by Samantha Schwartz and Zeya Grace, respectively), delivering not-so-age-appropriate lines and standing up to their mothers with a mix of sass and spunk.
Beaches accomplishes exactly what it sets out to do.
Beaches, the musical, is not bad but it is fatally misguided.
There is little here that feels an improvement on the movie, and several aspects that feel like a downgrade.
Beaches, A New Musical is a mostly forgettable endeavor
On Broadway, it largely misses the mark.
Instead, what unfolds is curiously muted.
The answer being: It's mildly okay.

Aside from the two leads, brash young Samantha Schwartz as brash young Cee Cee in flashbacks, and James Noone’s efficient and attractive jigsaw-piece-collage set, that’s pretty much it on the credit side of the ledger.
A mess as major as 'Beaches' required not one but two directors.
Gorgeous set design, the two most adorable child actresses to step into these roles, and the potency of its strong narrative carry Beaches through a few significant flaws.

Instead, an impressionistic painting frames the best friends in the musical's climactic scene. Vosk's effort to elevate the material is herculean, her charisma and humor often rising above Lonny Price and Matt Cowart's flat direction.
Naturally, he makes an awkward pass at a married Cee Cee — proving his boner fides — but Bertie stumbles on the scene and immediately misconstrues who's to blame.
Tell the management at Joe Allen to make space on the flop wall.

sg.ra: Center rows F-L sit just past the first-row neck-crane and just before the Row H mezz overhang bites. Sharp sightlines, clean sound, full set visible from deck to fly loft.
Panoramic top-down view with zero overhang and a steep-enough rake that no head blocks you. The better pick than center orchestra for big choreography or any show with stage-high spectacle.
Steep rake, no one in front of you, nothing cut off. You trade intimacy for a clean full-stage read at roughly a third of center-orchestra pricing.
Priced to move and close to the action, but outer seats clip the far side of the stage and you'll crane for anything upstage. Stay toward the aisle-adjacent seats or accept the compromise.

The front-mezz overhang starts clipping upstage action from Row H and fully buries anything high by Row P. You're paying mid-orchestra prices for a letterboxed view — rear mezz front rows beats this every time.

vr.q: So grab your best friend and go see beaches, a new musical on Broadway right now. I promise you're gonna wanna be there with them.
